metaDescription: Five cordless reciprocating saws under $100 compared on stroke length, brushless motors, one-handed designs, blades in the box and battery platform.
expertTake: A reciprocating saw is a demolition and pruning tool, and under $100 the useful question is how much stroke, vibration control and battery you get. The Makita XRJ04Z is the best overall with a 1-1/4 inch stroke and 0 to 2,800 SPM on the LXT platform, sold bare. The CORANEX kit is the best complete package with brushless power, two 4.0 Ah batteries, 11 blades and a case, and the Milwaukee Hackzall is the one-handed pick. Skip this tier if you cut cast iron pipe or rebar for a living.
introParagraphs: A reciprocating saw drives a stiff blade back and forth through wood, nails, pipe and branches, which makes it the tool people reach for when the work is rough and the angle is awkward. It is not precise, and it is not meant to be. What matters is how hard it bites and how much it shakes your arms.

This guide explains what a low price buys in a cordless reciprocating saw, why stroke length matters more than the headline speed and which kits include enough blades and battery to be useful. The quick picks are above, and the reviews below match each saw to a job.

products.name: Makita XRJ04Z 18V LXT Cordless Reciprocating Saw, Tool Only
products.description:
The XRJ04Z has the longest stroke in the group at 1-1/4 inches, which is a real mechanical advantage. Stroke length is the distance the blade travels each cycle, and a longer stroke pulls more teeth through the cut per stroke and clears chips better. That is why a saw with a modest 2,800 strokes per minute can still cut faster in a thick branch than a saw with a higher rate and a shorter stroke.

The variable-speed trigger gives you control at the start of a cut, where a blade tends to skate, and the tool-less blade change lets you swap blades without a key. Against the CORANEX and SEESII, which list 3,500 SPM, the Makita runs slower but with a longer stroke. It is sold bare, so you need an LXT battery. If you own one, this is the best value in this guide.

Because the saw is sold without blades and batteries, buy a pair of quality bimetal blades: a coarse one for wood and pruning, a fine one for metal. Brace the shoe against the work with firm pressure so the saw does not bounce, which is the main way to cut faster and reduce hand fatigue. For heavy demolition, pair it with a 6 inch bimetal demolition blade, and the long stroke will make short work of nailed framing.
products.bestFor: Makita owners and buyers who want the longest stroke and a durable platform.
pros: 1-1/4 inch stroke is the longest in the group
Variable speed trigger gives control at cut start
LXT battery fits a huge tool range
cons: Bare tool, so battery and charger cost extra
Lower stroke rate than the 3,500 SPM kits

products.name: CORANEX Brushless Cordless Reciprocating Saw, 2 x 4.0Ah, 11 Blades and Case
products.description:
The CORANEX is the most complete box: a brushless motor, two 4.0 Ah batteries, 11 blades and a carry case. A brushless motor wastes less energy as heat and typically gives longer run time per charge, which is important in a saw because reciprocating blades load a motor heavily. Two batteries mean one can charge while the other works, which turns a saw that runs for 20 minutes into one that works all day.

With 11 blades you can cut wood, nails, pipe and metal without extra purchases, which matters because blade choice decides what a reciprocating saw can do. Against the Makita, it gives up stroke length information, since the listing does not state it, but it offers a higher stroke rate and everything in the box.

Because it is a no-name platform, replacing a battery in three years may be difficult. Treat the packs as consumables and avoid storing them fully charged for months. The saw suits pruning, demolition of old framing and plumbing work, and it is light enough for one-handed use when the cut is easy. The case also makes it easy to store with the spare blades, which prevents the usual loss of the small blades in a drawer.
products.bestFor: First-time buyers who want everything in one box, including blades and a case.
pros: Two 4.0 Ah batteries for continuous work
Brushless motor with 3,500 SPM top rate
cons: Stroke length is not stated on the listing

products.name: SKIL PWR CORE 20 Brushless Compact Reciprocating Saw Kit, 2.0Ah USB-C

specList.label: Lighting
specList.value: Dual LEDs with pre-light and afterglow

products.description:
The SKIL is the best compact option because it builds in vibration control. A counterbalanced gearbox moves a weight opposite to the blade, so some of the shaking is cancelled before it reaches your hand. Reciprocating saws are brutal on wrists, and that feature is rare in a low-cost kit. A pivoting shoe also lets you rock the saw against the work to cut curves and keep the blade engaged.

The brushless motor reaches 3,000 SPM, and the dual LEDs light the cut with a pre-light and afterglow, which helps in attics and crawl spaces. The 2.0 Ah USB-C battery charges from a 45 W power-delivery charger, which is faster than many budget chargers but smaller than the CORANEX's 4.0 Ah packs. Compared with the CORANEX, the SKIL is a more refined tool with less battery and no blade assortment.

It is compact, so it fits between joists and studs, but a compact saw has a smaller motor and less reach. Use it for pruning, trim demolition and small plumbing. Keep blades sharp, because a dull blade shakes the saw and drains the battery. Its compact size is also a safety advantage in attic work, because you can keep a firm stance while cutting.
products.bestFor: People who cut in tight spaces and want less vibration.
pros: Dual LEDs light dark work areas
cons: 2.0 Ah battery is small for long jobs
No blade assortment in the kit

products.name: Milwaukee 2625-20 M18 Hackzall One-Handed Reciprocating Saw, Bare Tool
products.description:
The Hackzall is a different shape of saw: a one-handed, pistol-style tool for tight spaces. Where a full-size reciprocating saw needs two hands and a long body, the Hackzall fits between studs and above a ceiling grid. An anti-vibration handle is designed to reduce fatigue when ripping through heavier pieces, and the Quick-Lok clamp tightens and loosens with an on-board latch near the front.

It is a bare tool, so the M18 battery adds cost, but the M18 platform is one of the broadest, with hundreds of tools and plentiful spare packs. Compared with the Makita, it gives up stroke length and the lower stress of two-handed support, but it takes you into places the big saw cannot reach.

One-handed saws are best for plumbing, electrical and light demolition work, not for heavy cutting through thick lumber. A smaller body makes it easier to keep square in awkward positions, but it also means more bounce if you do not brace it. Use short blades and keep the shoe tight against the work. If you also own M18 tools, the shared battery makes this the least expensive way to add a second saw.
products.bestFor: Plumbers, electricians and renovators who work in tight spaces.
pros: M18 platform has a huge tool and battery range
cons: Bare tool, so battery and charger cost extra
Less cutting power than a full-size saw
Less control on heavy cuts than two hands

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 20V MAX BDCR20C Cordless Reciprocating Saw Kit
products.description:
The BDCR20C is the basic kit: a saw, a battery and a charger from a household brand. Its tool-free blade change, pivoting shoe and variable-speed trigger cover the features that matter most for light work such as pruning and cutting old trim. A pivoting shoe lets the shoe rock to follow the surface, which keeps the blade engaged in a curved cut.

It is designed for homeowners, and its main advantage is the POWERCONNECT platform, which shares batteries with a wide range of home tools. Compared with the SKIL and CORANEX it lacks a brushless motor on its listing and a larger battery, so it runs out of energy sooner and cuts more slowly.

Use it for pruning branches, cutting plastic pipe and removing trim. For demolition of framing or metal pipe, it will struggle. Replace the stock blade with a coarse pruning blade for branches or a bimetal blade for nails, because a general-purpose blade is a compromise. Treat it as a first reciprocating saw, and move up to a heavier model only if you find yourself running out of power.
products.bestFor: Homeowners who want a simple kit for pruning and light demolition.
pros: Complete kit with battery and charger
POWERCONNECT battery fits many home tools

buyingCriteria.explanation: The Makita XRJ04Z has a 1-1/4 inch stroke at up to 2,800 SPM, while the CORANEX reaches 3,500 SPM with an unlisted stroke. Longer strokes clear chips and cut thick material faster, so a slower saw with a longer stroke can cut faster in a log. Look for at least 1 inch of stroke for demolition or pruning. As a rule of thumb, 1-1/4 inch strokes suit demolition, while 3/4 inch strokes suit small plumbing work.

A reciprocating saw shakes your hands and arms, and the SKIL's counterbalanced gearbox and the Milwaukee's anti-vibration handle address this directly. Without such features, a long session leaves your forearms numb. A pivoting shoe, as on the SKIL and B+D, also keeps the saw steady. On a ladder, the weight of a full-size saw is a safety issue, so a compact saw is the safer tool for overhead work.

A coarse 6 TPI blade cuts wood and branches fast, while a fine 14 to 18 TPI bimetal blade cuts metal and nails. The CORANEX includes 11 blades, other kits fewer, and the Makita none. A stock blade is a compromise, so buy blades for your task. Check the clamp style, since a lever or twist clamp tightens faster than a screw-type one and wears less.

The Makita and Milwaukee are bare tools, while the CORANEX, SKIL and B+D include batteries. A bare tool is a deal only if you own the pack. The CORANEX's two 4.0 Ah batteries are a real advantage in a heavy-draw tool. A pair of 4.0 Ah batteries gives roughly twice the cutting time of the SKIL's single 2.0 Ah pack.

A full-size saw like the Makita gives more leverage and cutting power, while the Milwaukee Hackzall fits tight spaces. Choose by where you work. For roofs, attics and cabinets, one-handed wins. For felling branches and demolishing walls, full-size wins. The Milwaukee Hackzall also takes shorter blades, which are easier to control in cramped spaces.

Reciprocating saws load a motor heavily, so a brushless design like the CORANEX or SKIL makes less heat and gets more from the battery. If you cut for hours, it helps. For an occasional pruning job, a standard motor is acceptable. A brushless saw will also run quieter and cooler, which matters in an attic in summer.

specDecoder.meaning: SPM counts how many times the blade goes back and forth. A higher rate cuts faster in thin material. Stroke length times SPM does not give cutting speed, because blade geometry and tooth count also matter.
specDecoder.watchFor: A high SPM with a short stroke is not better than a lower SPM with a long stroke. Check both.

specDecoder.meaning: Stroke length is the distance the blade travels per stroke. The Makita's 1-1/4 inch is longer than most saws at this price. A longer stroke usually means a heavier saw.
specDecoder.watchFor: Many listings omit it. The CORANEX and SKIL do not state it.

specDecoder.meaning: A shoe that pivots lets you rock the saw against the surface to keep the blade in contact. A pivoting shoe lets you cut curved branches without rolling the saw off the bark.
specDecoder.watchFor: A fixed shoe can bounce on curved surfaces.

specDecoder.meaning: A counterweight moves opposite the blade to cancel vibration. Counterbalance mechanisms add weight and cost but reduce fatigue.
specDecoder.watchFor: Only the SKIL lists this feature here.

specDecoder.meaning: A clamp that releases the blade without a key saves time. A keyless clamp should still be checked for wear.
specDecoder.watchFor: Check that the clamp holds the blade firmly under load.

howWeEvaluated.title: Stroke and speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared stroke rate and length, giving the Makita credit for its 1-1/4 inch stroke and the CORANEX credit for 3,500 SPM. We listed stroke length wherever the maker gave it and noted where it was missing.

howWeEvaluated.title: Vibration and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: We rewarded counterbalance, anti-vibration handles and pivoting shoes. We assumed a homeowner doing pruning, trim demolition and small plumbing jobs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit contents
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted blades, batteries and cases, which decide whether a saw is useful out of the box. We credited kits that include batteries and blades because both are needed from day one.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor and battery
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored brushless motors and larger batteries. We considered how often each platform sells spare packs.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit across the lineup
howWeEvaluated.description: Each saw was placed by job, from pruning to tight-space work. We ranked by fit for each owner type.

howToChoose.intro: Match the saw to the work. Thick branches reward stroke length, while framing nails reward a bimetal blade and a steady shoe, so the Makita suits both better than the short-stroke kits.
howToChoose.note: Match the blade to the job before blaming the saw.

howToChoose.intro: Relative tiers in this group. Prices in this tier are close enough that the box contents, blades and batteries, usually decide the winner.
The shape of the saw matters. Many buyers assume a one-handed saw is just a smaller saw, but its pistol shape changes how you brace and steer the cut.

cards.label: Full-size
cards.text: The Makita and CORANEX give more leverage and fit heavy work like demolition and pruning.

cards.label: One-handed
cards.text: The Milwaukee Hackzall and the compact SKIL fit tight spaces and overhead work.

howToChoose.intro: The battery changes the cost. Batteries are the hidden cost, since a bare saw plus pack can cost more than a complete kit from a smaller brand.
Pruning needs a long stroke and a coarse blade. Pruning is mostly about reach and blade type, so a lightweight saw with a coarse blade beats a stronger saw that tires your arms.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A long stroke, a coarse 6 TPI pruning blade and a lightweight body for overhead cuts.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Makita's 1-1/4 inch stroke and the CORANEX's blade set make them best.

howToChoose.intro: Budget saws have limits. The cheapest recip saw is the one that matches your actual job, and the most expensive is the one that quits mid-cut.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You cut thick metal or demolish daily. A premium brushless saw lasts longer.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You prune a few times a year. The B+D or CORANEX will do.

maintenance.why: Debris jams clamps. Blow them clear. Pull the battery before changing blades.
A dull blade shakes the saw and drains the battery. Inspect the clamp for wear.
A loose shoe bounces. Tighten it. Wipe resin from the shoe.
Heat ages lithium cells. Cycle the battery occasionally.
Blocked vents overheat the motor. Store the saw dry.

faq.q: Can a cordless reciprocating saw replace a corded one?
faq.a: For pruning and light demolition, yes. For long heavy cuts, a corded saw runs longer. Always clamp or brace the work and keep both hands on the saw when you can.
Use a coarse blade for wood, a bimetal blade for nails and a fine blade for metal. Let the blade stop fully before you pull it out of the cut.
Yes. A longer stroke clears chips and cuts thick material faster. Wear eye protection, since broken blades and chips fly.
If you work in tight spaces, yes. For heavy cuts, a full-size saw is better. A fresh pack should be charged fully before the first job and then stored cool.

faq.q: How many batteries do I need?
faq.a: Two. One works while the other charges. If your cut binds, back the blade out slightly and restart rather than forcing it.

faq.q: Do I need to brace the saw?
faq.a: Yes. Press the shoe firmly against the work to reduce bounce. Keep hands clear of the blade path, and never saw toward a hidden wire or pipe.
